extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques and basic discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing and checking elementary proofs: induction (ordinary and strong), proof by smallest counterexample, proofs about Fibonacci numbers, and definitions/properties of relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive, equivalence).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use strong induction when the k+1 case depends on the truth of the statement for multiple smaller values m ≤ k (not merely for k). Example: in the tree-with-n-vertices proof, removing one edge produces two smaller trees whose sizes may be less than k, so the inductive hypothesis must be available for all m ≤ k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly: 'it was absolutely essential that we used strong induction ... because the two trees T1 and T2 will not both have k vertices. At least one will have fewer than k vertices. Thus the statement Sk is not enough to imply Sk+1. We need to use the assumption that Sm will be true whenever m ≤ k, and strong induction allows us to do this.' Practical check: if the inductive step decomposes the object into subobjects of varying sizes, prefer strong induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for proof by smallest counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'All S_n are true' by smallest counterexample: (1) Check S1 is true. (2) Suppose not every S_n is true. (3) Let k>1 be the smallest integer for which S_k is false. (4) Then S_{k-1} is true and S_k is false; use this collision to derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a hybrid of induction and contradiction that forces a direct contradiction from the existence of the smallest false case. The method is 'automatic' in that once you assume a smallest counterexample, you get S_{k-1} true and S_k false and should use those facts to build the contradiction. Numbering steps in exposition is optional in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply smallest counterexample to divisibility proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Example application: prove 4 | (5^n − 1) for all n. Check base case n=1, suppose there is a smallest k>1 with 4 ∤ (5^k − 1), use that 4 | (5^{k−1} − 1) to write 5^{k−1} − 1 = 4a and algebraically deduce 5^k − 1 = 4(5a+1), contradicting the assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique pattern: (a) assume smallest counterexample k; (b) use truth of smaller cases (often k−1) to express earlier term in divisible form; (c) manipulate to show the supposedly false case is actually true. Useful for many arithmetic divisibility statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy for Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove existence of a prime factorization by strong induction (show every n>1 has a prime factorization). Prove uniqueness by proof by smallest counterexample: assume smallest n with two distinct prime factorizations, use divisibility of primes to cancel a common prime and contradict minimality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence: base case n=2, then for n+1 if composite write n+1=ab and apply inductive hypothesis to a and b, concatenating their prime factorizations. Uniqueness: assume smallest counterexample, note a prime factor of one factorization must equal a prime in the other (use proposition that primes dividing a product divide a factor), divide through and use minimality to force contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction vs strong induction (general guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary induction assumes Sk and proves Sk+1; strong induction assumes Sm for all m ≤ k and proves Sk+1. Use ordinary induction when the k+1 case reduces only to the k case; use strong induction when k+1 reduces to several smaller cases or to cases smaller than k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text illustrates necessity of strong induction with the tree-splitting example. When the inductive step requires assumptions about more than the immediate predecessor (e.g., Fibonacci recurrence Fn depends on two previous terms), use strong induction or a suitably framed inductive hypothesis (often with multiple base cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibonacci induction guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving identities about Fibonacci numbers, expect to use the recurrence Fn = Fn−1 + Fn−2 (or equivalently Fn+1 = Fn + Fn−1) somewhere in the inductive step. Typically base cases include the first two terms, and the inductive step uses the recurrence to reduce higher-index expressions to earlier ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove F_{n+1}^2 − F_{n+1}F_n − F_n^2 = (−1)^n one checks base case n=1, assumes the identity for k, and then expands F_{k+2} using the recurrence and algebraically reduces to −(−1)^k = (−1)^{k+1}. For Fibonacci problems one often needs two base cases and a hypothesis that covers the two preceding indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a relation on a set
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation on a set A is a subset R ⊆ A × A. The pair (x,y) ∈ R is abbreviated xRy; (x,y) ∉ R is x R y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat relations as sets of ordered pairs; many familiar relations (e.g., <, =, congruence modulo n) can be expressed this way. This formal viewpoint allows set operations (intersection, union, complement) to produce new relations and supports definitions and proofs about relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to represent relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations can be described as explicit sets of ordered pairs, by set-builder notation, or by diagrams that place elements as nodes and draw an arrow from x to y iff (x,y) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose representation based on clarity: finite relations often suit diagrams; infinite relations require set-builder notation. Diagrams help visualize properties but are impractical for infinite sets. Examples in the text include listing pairs for small finite sets and drawing arrows for pictorial understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive property
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is reflexive if xRx for every x ∈ A (i.e., ∀ x ∈ A, (x,x) ∈ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ≤, =, and divisibility | are reflexive. Non-examples: <, > are not reflexive. In a diagram reflexivity is indicated by a loop at each vertex. To prove reflexivity, show for arbitrary x that the defining condition yields xRx (e.g., for congruence mod n, n|(x−x)=0 so x ≡ x (mod n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric property
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is symmetric if xRy implies yRx for all x,y ∈ A (i.e., ∀ x,y, (x,y)∈R ⇒ (y,x)∈R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: equality = and congruence modulo n are symmetric. Non-examples: ≤ is not symmetric. In diagrams symmetry is indicated by each arrow being paired by an arrow in the opposite direction. To prove symmetry directly, assume xRy and manipulate the defining condition to deduce yRx (e.g., if n|(x−y) then n|(y−x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive property
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation R on A is transitive if whenever xRy and yRz then xRz for all x,y,z ∈ A (i.e., ∀ x,y,z, (x,y)∈R ∧ (y,z)∈R ⇒ (x,z)∈R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ≤, <, =, and divisibility | are transitive. In diagrams transitivity means that whenever there is a path of length two from x to z via y, there must be a direct arrow from x to z; in particular if xRy and yRx in a transitive relation then loops at x and y follow. To prove transitivity, start with the two hypotheses and combine them (e.g., add congruence relations: if n|(x−y) and n|(y−z) then n|(x−z)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting relation properties in diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual tests: reflexive = loop at each point; symmetric = for every arrow x→y there is an arrow y→x; transitive = whenever arrows x→y and y→z exist, also x→z exists (including the implied loops when x=z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook provides illustrative diagrams and notes limitations: diagrams help for small finite relations but are inadequate for infinite relations (e.g., congruence mod n). Use diagrams as an aid to intuition, then give formal proofs when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (definition and checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: An equivalence relation on A is one that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Equivalence relations partition A into equivalence classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To check an equivalence relation, verify the three properties. The text gives multiple example relations (e.g., equality, same parity, same sign) and lists their ordered-pair descriptions and equivalence classes. Use equivalence classes to describe the partition induced by the relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruence modulo n is reflexive (n|(x−x)), symmetric (n|(x−y) ⇒ n|(y−x)), and transitive (n|(x−y) and n|(y−z) ⇒ n|(x−z) by adding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives step-by-step direct proofs for each property. This is the model for proving algebraic relations are equivalence relations: use the algebraic definition (divisibility) and basic arithmetic manipulations (multiply by −1, add equations) to establish the properties.
